pos: n. (the stirring of lawsuits; also a shipmaster's fraud against the owners)
etymology: From an old word for quarrel and barter. Webster: the practice of exciting and encouraging lawsuits and quarrels. In commerce, fraud by a shipmaster that injures the owners or insurers.
biblical_def:
Only by pride cometh contention: but with the well advised is wisdom. A fool's lips enter into contention, and his mouth calleth for strokes. Avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.

Barratry is the trade of starting fights other men must pay to finish. Scripture does not use the statute word. It does name the pride that produces contention, and the fool whose lips enter it. Webster's second sense, the master who sinks the ship or takes the cargo, is theft inside a trust. Both senses profit by damaging what was put in a man's hands.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the practice of exciting and encouraging lawsuits and quarrels. In commerce, cheating or fraud by a shipmaster by which the owners or insurers are injured.
webster_full: BARRATRY, n. The practice of exciting and encouraging lawsuits and quarrels.
In commerce, any species of cheating or fraud in a shipmaster, by which the owners or insurers are injured; as by running away with the ship, sinking or deserting her, or by embezzling the cargo.
scriptures: Only by pride cometh contention: but with the well advised is wisdom.
Pro 18:6
A fool's lips enter into contention, and his mouth calleth for strokes.
Tit 3:9
But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.
corruption_summary: The age treats a stirred lawsuit as advocacy, and a faithless shipmaster as a victim of the sea.
corruption_paragraphs: Titus 3:9 calls the stirred contention unprofitable and vain. A man who lives by encouraging quarrels is a dealer in strife, not a defender of the injured.
The commercial sense belongs with embezzlement. Deserting the ship or taking the cargo is not weather. It is a broken trust.
roots_summary: No biblical headword. The field is contention from pride (Pro 13:10) and fraud in a trust.
roots_lines: Exciting lawsuits is the first sense. Pride is the biblical source.
The shipmaster's fraud is the second sense. The cargo was not his.
usage: Only by pride cometh contention — the root under the barrator.
Avoid contentions and strivings about the law — the apostolic ban on hired strife.

pos: n. (a bargain to carry another's suit for a share of what is recovered)
etymology: A species of maintenance. Webster: a bargain with a plaintiff or defendant to divide the matter in suit if they prevail, the champertor carrying the suit at his own expense. The purchase of a suit, or of the right of suing.
biblical_def:
Thou shalt not wrest judgment. A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment. He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.

Champerty buys a piece of another man's case. The buyer does not come as a witness. He comes as an owner of the verdict. Scripture forbids the gift that blinds the wise and perverts the words of the righteous. A share of the recovery, bargained before the judgment, is that gift wearing a contract.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a bargain with a plaintiff or defendant to divide the land or other matter in suit if they prevail, the champertor carrying the suit at his own expense. The purchase of a suit, or of the right of suing.
webster_full: CHAMPERTY, n. A species of maintenance, being a bargain with a plaintiff or defendant to divide the land or other matter in suit between them, if they prevail.
Whereupon the champertor is to carry on the party's suit at his own expense.
The purchase of a suit, or of the right of suing.
scriptures: Thou shalt not wrest judgment; thou shalt not respect persons, neither take a gift: for a gift doth blind the eyes of the wise, and pervert the words of the righteous.
A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.
corruption_summary: The age calls the purchase of a lawsuit an investment, so that a bought share of another man's verdict looks like business.
corruption_paragraphs: Deuteronomy 16:19 does not ask what the gift is called. A gift that blinds the wise is forbidden. A contracted share of the recovery is a gift with a percentage.
Proverbs 17:15 names the end. Justifying the wicked and condemning the just are both abomination. Champerty aims at that end for a fee.
roots_summary: No biblical headword. The field is a gift that perverts judgment (Deu 16:19; Pro 17:23).
roots_lines: The purchase of a right to sue is Webster's last line. Scripture already forbids buying the judgment.
A share bargained before the verdict is not charity to a poor kinsman. It is ownership of the case.
usage: A gift doth blind the eyes of the wise — the statute under a bought suit.
A wicked man taketh a gift out of the bosom to pervert the ways of judgment.

pos: n. (a corrupt attempt to influence a jury)
etymology: From an old word for influencing by embrace, promise, or entertainment. Webster: an attempt to influence a jury corruptly to one side, by promises, persuasions, entreaties, money, entertainments, or the like.
biblical_def:
Thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous. Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment. Do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men?

Embracery is the corrupting of the men who are to say what is true. The gift, the meal, the promise, the pressure of the many — Scripture names each of them. A jury influenced to one side has already left the duty to justify the righteous and condemn the wicked.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): an attempt to influence a jury corruptly to one side, by promises, persuasions, entreaties, money, entertainments, or the like.
webster_full: EMBRACERY, n. In law, an attempt to influence a jury corruptly to one side, by promises, persuasions, entreaties, money, entertainments, or the like.
scriptures: Exo 23:8
And thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise, and perverteth the words of the righteous.
Exo 23:2
Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment:
Psa 58:1
Do ye indeed speak righteousness, O congregation? do ye judge uprightly, O ye sons of men?
corruption_summary: The age treats pressure on a jury as messaging, so long as the money is called hospitality.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 23:8 does not exempt an entertainment. The gift blinds. Webster lists entertainments with money and promises.
Exodus 23:2 forbids declining after many to wrest judgment. A crowd leaned on a jury is the same sin as a purse.
roots_summary: No biblical headword. The field is the gift that blinds (Exo 23:8) and the multitude followed to wrest judgment (Exo 23:2).
roots_lines: Corruptly to one side is Webster's point. The aim is not truth. It is a side.
Psalm 58:1 asks the congregation if it judges uprightly. Embracery answers no, and hides the no.
usage: Thou shalt take no gift: for the gift blindeth the wise.
Neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment.

pos: n. (evil doing; a wrong or illegal deed, especially in an office)
etymology: From mal, evil, and feasance, a doing. Webster: evil doing; wrong; illegal deed.
biblical_def:
Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed. Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds. Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?

Malfeasance is a wrong done in the doing of an office. The decree, the bed-plot, the law framed for mischief — Scripture does not require a Latin name. The officer who uses the pen of his office to injure is doing evil, and the woe is already written.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): evil doing; wrong; illegal deed.
webster_full: MALFEASANCE, n. Evil doing; wrong; illegal deed.
scriptures: Isa 10:1
Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees, and that write grievousness which they have prescribed;
Mic 2:1
Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand.
Shall the throne of iniquity have fellowship with thee, which frameth mischief by a law?
corruption_summary: The age treats an illegal deed in office as a process error, so long as a form was filed.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 10:1 puts the woe on the decree itself. A prescribed grievousness is not sanitized by the office that wrote it.
Micah 2:1 names the power of the hand. Malfeasance is evil that can be practised because the office supplies the power.
roots_summary: No biblical headword. The field is the unrighteous decree (Isa 10:1) and mischief framed by a law (Psa 94:20).
roots_lines: Evil doing is Webster's whole definition. The office does not change the adjective.
Psalm 94:20 asks if the throne of iniquity can have fellowship with God. The answer is no.
usage: Woe unto them that decree unrighteous decrees.
Which frameth mischief by a law — malfeasance wearing a statute.

pos: n. (the embezzlement of public money or goods entrusted for disbursement)
etymology: Latin peculari, to embezzle. Webster: the act or crime of defrauding the public by appropriating to one's own use the money or goods entrusted to one's care for management or disbursement.
biblical_def:
Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity. And kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it. The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again.

Peculation is embezzlement when the trust is public. The money was given to be disbursed. The hand kept it. Scripture does not excuse the theft because the purse belonged to the congregation or the city rather than to one neighbour. Fidelity is the duty. Keeping back part is the crime.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the crime of defrauding the public by appropriating to one's own use the money or goods entrusted to one's care for management or disbursement; embezzlement of public money or goods.
webster_full: PECULATION, n. The act, practice or crime of defrauding the public by appropriating to one's own use the money or goods entrusted to one's care for management or disbursement.
Embezzlement of public money or goods.
scriptures: Tit 2:10
Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.
Act 5:2
And kept back part of the price, his wife also being privy to it, and brought a certain part, and laid it at the apostles' feet.
The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth.
corruption_summary: The age calls peculation a discrepancy in a public account, so that a trusted theft of the common purse keeps the name of administration.
corruption_paragraphs: Titus 2:10 does not limit fidelity to a private master. Purloining adorns nothing. A public purse is still a trust.
Ananias kept back part and laid the rest down as if it were the whole. Peculation often wears that shape: a partial return offered as a full accounting.
roots_summary: Latin peculari, to embezzle. The biblical field is purloining (Tit 2:10) and keeping back part (Act 5:2).
roots_lines: Public money does not change the eighth commandment. It aggravates the trust.
Acts 5:2 is the church's exhibit of a kept-back portion.
usage: Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity.
Kept back part of the price — peculation that still looks like a gift.

pos: n. (a cutting off; a deduction; also the taking of a part that was not one's own)
etymology: Latin defalcare, to cut off with a sickle. Webster: the act of cutting off or deducting a part; diminution; abatement. Also that which is cut off.
biblical_def:
Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it. The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again. Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity.

Defalcation, in Webster's plain sense, is a cutting off of a part. A just deduction, named and agreed, is one thing. A cut taken from what is due to another, and not confessed, is theft by subtraction. Scripture requires the good that is due to be given when the hand can give it. A silent defalcation is the opposite.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): the act of cutting off, or deducting a part; deduction; diminution; abatement. Also that which is cut off.
webster_full: DEFALCATION, n. The act of cutting off, or deducting a part; deduction; diminution; abatement.
scriptures: Pro 3:27
Withhold not good from them to whom it is due, when it is in the power of thine hand to do it.
The wicked borroweth, and payeth not again: but the righteous sheweth mercy, and giveth.
Tit 2:10
Not purloining, but shewing all good fidelity; that they may adorn the doctrine of God our Saviour in all things.
corruption_summary: The age uses defalcation as a soft name for a taken part, so that a cut from what is due sounds like accounting.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster's honest sense is a named deduction. The corruption is the unnamed cut. Proverbs 3:27 does not permit the hand to withhold good that is due.
A ledger that shows a smaller sum than was entrusted, without a true abatement, is purloining. The softer noun does not change the act.
roots_summary: Latin defalcare, to cut off. The moral test is whether the cut was due, or withheld (Pro 3:27).
roots_lines: A true abatement is declared. A defalcation that hides is a taking.
Titus 2:10 still governs the hand that manages another's goods.
usage: Withhold not good from them to whom it is due.
Not purloining — the rule a silent cut breaks.

pos: n. (the stain of blood, and the judgment of death that works forfeiture)
etymology: From Latin attingere, to touch or stain, through the law-French of attainder. Webster: literally a staining or corruption of blood. Hence the judgment of death upon treason or felony, which forfeits lands and disqualifies the convict. He notes that by the Constitution of the United States no crime works an attainder.
biblical_def:
The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son. He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.

Attainder, in the old law, stained the blood so that the children could not inherit. Scripture will not carry a father's treason into the son's title as a permanent corruption of blood. The soul that sinneth shall die. The son shall not bear the father's iniquity. A just court may punish the guilty man. It may not, by a stain on the blood, disinherit the innocent child as if the guilt were a breed.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): literally a staining or corruption of blood. The judgment of death upon treason or felony, which attaints the blood so that the convict can no longer inherit. By the Constitution of the United States, no crime works an attainder.
webster_full: ATTAINDER, n. Literally a staining, corruption, or rendering impure; a corruption of blood.
The judgment of death upon a person convicted of treason or felony, which corrupts his blood, so that he can no longer inherit lands.
By the constitution of the United States, no crime works an attainder.
scriptures: The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.
He that justifieth the wicked, and he that condemneth the just, even they both are abomination to the LORD.
corruption_summary: The age either revives a stain on the children for the father's crime, or denies that the guilty man himself may be judged.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 18:20 is the limit. The soul that sinneth dies. The son does not bear the father's iniquity. Attainder of blood crosses that line.

The other corruption is the refusal to condemn the guilty man at all. Proverbs 17:15 condemns both the false acquittal and the false condemnation. Abolishing judgment is not the cure for a corrupt stain.
roots_summary: Latin, a touching or staining. The biblical limit is Ezekiel 18:20: the son shall not bear the iniquity of the father.
roots_lines: Corruption of blood is the picture Webster keeps. Scripture refuses to make guilt hereditary in that legal sense.
The American Constitution, which Webster notes, agrees with Ezekiel on this point: no crime works an attainder.
usage: The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father — the verse that ends corruption of blood.
The soul that sinneth, it shall die — judgment on the guilty man, not on his breed.

pos: n. (a deceitful agreement between two to prejudice a third)
etymology: Law French, from an old word for a secret agreement. Webster: a collusive or deceitful agreement between two or more to prejudice a third person.
biblical_def:
They search out iniquities; they accomplish a diligent search: both the inward thought of every one of them, and the heart, is deep. Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds. Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.

Covin is a private agreement whose purpose is the injury of someone who is not in the room. Two mouths agree. A third man pays. Scripture calls that a deep heart and a devised iniquity. The agreement may wear the form of a contract. The prejudice of the absent man is the sin.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): a collusive or deceitful agreement between two or more to prejudice a third person.
webster_full: COVIN, n. In law, a collusive or deceitful agreement between two or more to prejudice a third person.
scriptures: Psa 64:6
They search out iniquities; they accomplish a diligent search: both the inward thought of every one of them, and the heart, is deep.
Mic 2:1
Woe to them that devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds! when the morning is light, they practise it, because it is in the power of their hand.
Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.
corruption_summary: The age calls a collusive agreement a deal, so long as the injured man was not invited to the table.
corruption_paragraphs: Psalm 64:6 names the inward thought. Covin is not an open controversy. It is a searched-out iniquity.
Micah 2:1 adds the morning practice. What was agreed on the bed is done when the hand has power. The absent third person is the one the agreement was built to hurt.
roots_summary: No biblical headword. The field is a devised iniquity (Mic 2:1) and a deep inward agreement (Psa 64:6).
roots_lines: Two against one is the shape. The third person is the victim of the accord.
False witness is the public face covin often wears when it reaches a court.
usage: The heart is deep — covin as an inward agreement.
They devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds — the plot before the morning.
